channel.title: Acme: Science Fiction and Fantasy News
channel.description: Science fiction and fantasy fandom news, publishing, conventions, and history.

item.title: Amazing Stories marks its centenary and remembers Steve Davidson
item.description: On November 18, 2026, Amazing Stories announced its Fall 2026 issue, volume 78, number 3 and whole number 623, as part of the magazine's centennial year. The issue also became a memorial to publisher Steve Davidson, who died on November 4 after helping restore the title to print in 2018. Its contents include new fiction by David Gerrold, Tom Easton and Dave Creek, alongside essays and art reflecting the magazine's long institutional history. For fandom historians, the conjunction is unusually pointed: the first science-fiction magazine is observing 100 years while documenting the loss of a steward responsible for its latest revival.

item.title: Prime Video confirms a fourth season of The Rings of Power
item.description: On November 24, 2026, Prime Video confirmed that The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power will return for a fourth season. The production is in pre-production at Shepperton Studios in the United Kingdom, with filming scheduled to begin in spring 2027; no release date or cast list has been announced. The renewal arrived as the final two episodes of season three became available, culminating in Sauron forging the One Ring. Amazon says all 24 episodes from the first three seasons are now streaming. The announcement settles the immediate future of one of fantasy television's largest adaptations while leaving its next creative team and timetable open.

item.title: Sarah Perry turns 47, a milestone for a modern Gothic fantasist
item.description: November 28, 2026, marks the 47th birthday of British novelist Sarah Perry, born in Chelmsford on November 28, 1979. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction entry, last updated November 10, 2025, predates this birthday peg but provides the relevant career record. Perry moved from the uncanny family history of After Me Comes the Flood through the historical and folkloric textures of The Essex Serpent, Melmoth and Enlightenment. Her fiction repeatedly tests faith, reason, haunting and social constraint without settling comfortably into one genre shelf. The date offers a useful occasion to revisit a writer whose work has helped return Gothic modes to the center of contemporary British literary fantasy.

item.title: Audible sets December 31 deadline for new royalty agreements
item.description: On November 26, 2026, The Bookseller reported that Audible is requiring rights holders to accept revised royalty agreements for each title by December 31 or lose distribution on the platform. The new structure shifts payments toward listening engagement and changes terms for both exclusive and nonexclusive ACX releases. Audible says creators' combined royalties rose 26 percent in the first two months of testing and that 64 percent of participants earned more, while acknowledging that results vary by title. The deadline and title-by-title acceptance requirement make this a consequential contract change for genre authors, small presses and audio producers whose backlists depend on Audible's reach.

item.title: Kirkus names its best science fiction and fantasy books of 2026
item.description: Kirkus Reviews' 2026 best science fiction and fantasy list, released as part of its November 15 Best Books issue and highlighted again on November 26, names eleven titles spanning major and independent voices. Selections include Dead Beat by Leigh Bardugo, The Faith of Beasts by James S. A. Corey, Mazywood by Tananarive Due, A Wall Is Also a Road by Annalee Newitz, What We Are Seeking by Cameron Reed, Green City Wars by Adrian Tchaikovsky and All the Hidden Places by Cadwell Turnbull. The mix offers fandom a compact snapshot of what one influential reviewing institution considered the year's strongest speculative fiction, with space opera, hard science fiction, urban fantasy and formally adventurous work all represented.

item.title: Scrooge reaches its 75th anniversary with Belfast screening
item.description: The Belfast Film Festival is marking the 75th anniversary of Brian Desmond Hurst's Scrooge, released in Britain on November 30, 1951, with a December 9, 2026 screening at Queen's University Belfast. The current festival listing reconnects the enduring Charles Dickens adaptation to Hurst's Belfast origins and describes Alastair Sim's performance as Ebenezer Scrooge as era-defining. The anniversary is more than seasonal programming: Hurst, born in east Belfast in 1895, learned filmmaking alongside John Ford and became one of Northern Ireland's most prolific directors. AFI records the film's original British title as Scrooge and its American release as A Christmas Carol, making the screening a well-pegged celebration of fantasy-film history.

item.title: Titan Books acquires two RR Khashman fantasy novels
item.description: On November 25, 2026, The Bookseller reported that Titan Books acquired world English-language rights to two novels by Future Worlds Prize-shortlisted author Rakan Khashman, writing as RR Khashman. Commissioning editor Daniel Carpenter bought the rights from James McGowan at BookEnds Literary Agency; Penguin Random House Audio separately acquired audio rights. The debut, With Death and Dance, is scheduled for July 2028. Set in a Venetian-inspired city, it follows two cursed thieves whose attempted robbery becomes a murder mystery after their intended victim is found dead. The deal is notable both as a two-book commitment to a debut writer and as another example of Titan’s continued investment in secondary-world fantasy with a strong crime-story engine.

item.title: Inaugural Children’s Booker names its ‘Great Eight’ shortlist
item.description: The Booker Prize Foundation announced the inaugural Children’s Booker Prize shortlist on November 24, 2026. The eight books, spanning novels, graphic novels and illustrated stories for readers ages eight to 12, include work by Guy Bass, Catherine Bruton, Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, Iqbal Hussain, Liz Hyder, Mikey Please, Jessica Scott-Whyte and Shaun Tan. Four child judges chosen from more than 4,000 applicants will join the adult panel in selecting the winner, to be announced February 2, 2027. Each shortlisted book receives £2,500, while the winner receives £50,000. For genre readers, the list’s mix of fantasy, time travel, monsters and otherworldly visitors makes the new institution worth watching from its first year.

item.title: Former Dragon Con co-founder Edward Kramer sentenced to prison
item.description: Gwinnett County announced on November 17, 2026, that Edward Kramer was sentenced to 40 years, with the first five in prison, after a judge revoked his first-offender status for probation violations. Kramer had entered a 2013 plea on three child-molestation counts stemming from his 2000 arrest. Prosecutors said the violations included photographing a child, contacting young males through social media and viewing pornography involving young males. Kramer co-founded Dragon Con but has had no connection to the convention or its organization since a 2013 cash-out merger. The sentence is a consequential development in a case that shadowed Atlanta fandom and Dragon Con for years; the county’s release is the primary official account of the hearing and punishment.

item.title: Karen Lansdale, writer and artist, dies at 74
item.description: On November 24, 2026, Locus reported the death of writer and artist Karen Lansdale, who died November 1 at age 74 from complications of Alzheimer’s disease. Lansdale collaborated with her husband, Joe R. Lansdale, on “A Change of Lifestyle” (1984) and “Screwup” (1999), supplied the ending to the family collaboration In Waders from Mars (2012), and created the cover art for Miracles Ain’t What They Used to Be (2016). The belated public notice is the current news peg, distinct from the November 1 death date. Her record is compact but entwined with one of modern fantastic fiction’s most recognizable literary families, making the details useful to readers tracking the less-visible collaborators who shape genre careers.

item.title: FanFiAddict launches boutique genre imprint FFA Publishing
item.description: FanFiAddict announced FFA Publishing on November 18, 2026, creating a boutique publishing arm devoted to fantasy, science fiction and horror anthologies financed through crowdfunding campaigns. Authors and podcasters Adrian M. Gibson and David Walters will lead the imprint, extending a network that already includes the SFF Addicts podcast, TBRCon and The Book of Spores. The announcement is the time peg; individual books, editors and contributors have not yet been disclosed, so the significance is institutional rather than a catalog launch. For fandom observers, the move is a fresh example of a review-and-podcast community converting its audience and convention experience into publishing infrastructure, with Kickstarter-style backing positioned as part of the model from the outset.

item.title: Children of the Nameless enters print with a charity tie-in
item.description: Subterranean Press highlighted the print debut of Brandon Sanderson’s Children of the Nameless on November 15, 2026, saying fewer than 10 percent of the trade-hardcover run remained and that part of the proceeds would benefit Child’s Play Charity. Sanderson originally released the Magic: The Gathering novella free through Wizards of the Coast in 2018; the new physical edition is therefore the current publishing peg, not a claim that the story itself is new. The project crosses several established fandom institutions—licensed game fiction, a major fantasy author, a specialty press and a games-oriented children’s charity—while turning a once-digital promotional work into a collectible book. That combination makes the edition more notable than a routine stock notice.

item.title: The Red Winter wins the 2026 Speakies science-fiction and fantasy prize
item.description: The British Audio Awards announced on November 24 that Cameron Sullivan’s The Red Winter, narrated by Rory Barnett and Imogen Church, won Best Audiobook: Science Fiction & Fantasy at the second annual Speakies. The ceremony took place November 23 at London’s Queen Elizabeth Hall and recognized audiobooks, drama, podcasts, performers and production. The category’s shortlist also included Femme Feral, Ice, King of Ravens, The Last Starborn Seer and There Is No Antimemetics Division. PodcastingToday’s November 24 report supplies the current news peg and identifies the winner. For genre readers, the result is also a useful marker of how performance, translation and production are gaining institutional recognition alongside print publishing.

item.title: Star Trek’s first two-part story reaches its 60th anniversary
item.description: “The Menagerie, Part II” first aired on November 24, 1966, making November 24, 2026 its 60th anniversary. The conclusion resolved Spock’s court-martial by reusing substantial footage from “The Cage,” the unaired original Star Trek pilot starring Jeffrey Hunter as Captain Christopher Pike. That production expedient preserved material viewers otherwise would not see in full for decades and created a durable bridge between the Pike and Kirk eras. The episode also became the only original-series story to receive the Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation. Paramount’s episode page documents the original broadcast date and premise; its date is the historical source date, while the anniversary is the current peg. The milestone invites another look at how scarcity and reuse became franchise mythology.

item.title: Doctor Who’s The Deadly Assassin finale turns 50
item.description: The fourth and final episode of Doctor Who’s “The Deadly Assassin” premiered on November 20, 1976, placing its 50th anniversary in the week of November 20, 2026. Robert Holmes’s serial sent the Fourth Doctor to Gallifrey without a companion, returned the Master in a decayed form, and transformed the Time Lords from remote demigods into a fallible political establishment. Its Matrix sequences and contested portrayal of Gallifreyan society became reference points for later television, novels and fan debate. The official Doctor Who episode guide records all four 1976 premiere dates; that historical broadcast date, rather than the 2026 anniversary, is used here as the source publication date. Half a century later, the serial’s institutional satire remains central to the program’s mythology.
